title: Numbers & shopping
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: A number decides the shape of the noun after it, which English never does. After odín the noun is in its ordinary dictionary shape (odín rubl'). After dva, tri and chetýre it takes one ending (dva rublyá). After pyat' and everything above it takes another (pyat' rubléy, sto rubléy). Learn the three shapes of a word you will count — rubl' · rublyá · rubléy — rather than trying to build them.
M4 already showed you this rule on the clock: odín chas, dva chasá, sem' chasóv. It was the same law then, applied to hours instead of roubles.

The price question agrees with the THING, not with the buyer: Skól'ko stóit kníga? for one, Skól'ko stóyat knígi? for more than one. M9's mne nrávitsya works the same way — a Russian verb very often agrees with the thing rather than with the person, and this is the first place it bites.

There is no everyday verb "to have". Possession is built out of a place phrase: U menyá yest' kníga is literally "at me is a book" — the owner sits in the U-phrase and the thing owned is the SUBJECT of the sentence. Russian does have a verb imét', but it is bookish and abstract and nobody uses it for owning a book, so Ya iméyu knígu is not so much wrong as unnatural.

U vas yest' …? is how you ask a shop whether they have something, and U menyá yest' … is how you say what you have. Learn each as one whole phrase: the yest' inside them is M7's existential word doing a second job.

Dáyte is the polite "give" — the vy-form, matching the register this course speaks throughout — and it is the only command this level teaches. It is nearly always followed by pozháluysta, set off by commas.

sentences.cue: How much does the book cost?

words.note: Two words, learned whole: skól'ko is "how much" and stóit is "costs". This is the one-thing version — S02 has the version for more than one. There is no do and no does anywhere in the question.

sentences.trap: English builds the question with a helper — "how much DOES it cost" — and Russian has nothing to build it with. The words of the statement, in order, plus a question mark.
sentences.sound: SKOL-ka STO-eet KNEE-ga. The l of skól'ko is soft, and both unstressed o letters flatten to "a".

variations.cue: How much does a ticket cost?
variations.changed: swap the thing priced — still one of it, so still stóit

variations.cue: How much does the milk cost?
variations.changed: a neuter thing this time, and the verb does not notice gender — only number

variations.cue: The book costs a hundred roubles
variations.changed: the answer, with the same verb and a price after it

mistake.why: Two things at once: nothing needs to be added to make a question, and yest' is not a helper. Skól'ko stóit kníga?

sentences.usage: Every shop, every market, every ticket office.
sentences.mnemonic: How much costs the thing. The words are already in the right order.

sentences.cue: How much do the books cost?

words.note: The more-than-one version. The verb changes because the THING is plural, not because the person asking has changed: stóit for one, stóyat for several. Nothing about the buyer appears in the sentence at all.

sentences.trap: In English "does" and "do" also follow the thing, so the idea is familiar — but it is worth naming, because M9's mne nrávitsya / mne nrávyatsya runs on the same principle and there English does the opposite.
sentences.sound: SKOL-ka sta-YAT KNEE-gee. The stress moves onto the ending in stóyat, which is why it sounds so unlike stóit.

variations.cue: How much does the book cost?
variations.changed: back to one book — stóyat → stóit, following the thing

variations.cue: How much do the tickets cost?
variations.changed: swap the plural thing — stóyat stays

variations.cue: The books cost a hundred roubles
variations.changed: the answer, with the same plural verb

mistake.why: knígi is more than one book, so the verb has to be stóyat. The verb follows the thing, always.

sentences.usage: Asking about several things at once — and the plural of a noun you already know is often just -i or -y.
sentences.mnemonic: The verb looks at what is being priced, never at who is asking.

sentences.cue: The book costs a hundred roubles

words.note: "Costs" — the verb inside S01's and S02's question phrases, here on its own in the answer. It follows the THING, not the buyer: stóit for one, stóyat for more than one. There is no "for" and no "is worth" anywhere: the price simply follows the verb.
A hundred. Three letters, and it never changes shape here — but like every number above four, it puts the noun behind it into the same shape pyat' does — rubléy, chasóv.

The rouble, in the three shapes the counting rule needs: odín rubl', dva rublyá, pyat' rubléy. Note that rubl' ends in -' and is masculine — M1 warned that -' nouns go either way and have to be learned one at a time.

sentences.trap: English says "a hundred roubles" with the noun untouched; Russian bends it. The number is in charge of the noun, and that is the whole grammar of this rung.
sentences.sound: KNEE-ga STO-eet sto roob-LYEY. The ' inside rubléy softens the l, and the stress lands on the ending.

variations.changed: after odín the noun is in its plain dictionary shape
dva takes the middle shape — rublyá, not rubléy

variations.cue: The ticket costs a hundred roubles
variations.changed: swap what is priced — the number and the noun behind it do not move

mistake.why: rubl' is the shape that follows odín. After sto it is rubléy.

sentences.usage: Every price you will be told — and the three shapes are worth learning as a set.
sentences.mnemonic: 1 plain, 2–4 one ending, 5 and up another. Three shapes cover every price in Russia.

words.note: Five — the number where the second ending starts. Everything from pyat' upward behaves the same way, so this one number teaches the whole upper half of the rule. It ends in -', like every number from five to twenty.

sentences.trap: There is nothing special about five in itself. It is simply where Russian's counting rule switches, and it stays switched for every number above it.
sentences.sound: sok STO-eet pyat' roob-LYEY. The ya of pyat' is a soft "a", and the ' on the end softens the t.

variations.changed: dva is in the 2–4 group, so the noun takes the other ending
swap what is priced — the number phrase is unchanged

variations.cue: How much does the juice cost?
variations.changed: the question this sentence answers

mistake.why: rublyá is the 2–4 shape. After pyat' it is rubléy.

sentences.usage: Any price under a hundred — and pyat' is the number to test the rule with.
sentences.mnemonic: Five is where the switch is. Above it, nothing changes again.

words.note: Three words, learned whole: "at you is …". There is no verb "to have" in it — the owner sits in the U-phrase and the thing owned is the subject. The yest' inside it is M7's existential word, doing possession instead of location. Ask a shop this and you have asked whether they stock it.

sentences.trap: Every instinct says to look for a Russian "have". There is not one in everyday use, and the sentence is built the other way round: the bread is the subject, and you are a place it might be found.
sentences.sound: oo vas yest' khlyep. Four short words, and the pitch rises on khleb to make the question.

variations.changed: swap what you are asking for — the phrase never moves
the thing owned is the subject, so it stays in its dictionary shape — kníga, not knígu
vas → menyá: the same frame, about yourself

mistake.why: imét' is a real verb, but a bookish one — nobody uses it for having bread. The everyday question is U vas yest' khleb?

sentences.usage: Every shop, every kitchen, every time you need something.
sentences.mnemonic: Russian does not have things. Things are AT you.

words.note: The same three-word frame about yourself. menyá is M1's ya in its object shape, and the phrase is literally "at me is …". The thing owned stays in its dictionary shape, because it is the subject of the sentence — bilét, never biléta.

sentences.trap: The thing you own does NOT take M3's object ending, because it is not an object — it is the subject. U menyá yest' kníga, never U menyá yest' knígu.
sentences.sound: oo mee-NYA yest' bee-LYET. menyá here sounds exactly as it did in Menyá zovút, because it is the same word.

variations.changed: swap what you have — and it stays in its dictionary shape
the most useful version of this sentence you will ever say
menyá → vas: the same frame, asked of somebody else

mistake.why: The thing owned is the subject of the sentence, so it keeps its dictionary shape: bilét.

sentences.usage: Saying what you have on you — tickets, keys, money, time.
sentences.mnemonic: At me is a ticket. The ticket is the subject; you are only the place.

words.note: "Give" — the vy-form, which is what makes it polite, and the only command this course teaches. The -te on the end is the same polite ending as on Zdrávstvuyte. With pozháluysta after it, it is the ordinary way to ask for something in a shop; without it, it is brusque.

sentences.trap: The thing asked for takes M3's object ending — vódu, not vodá — because Dáyte is a real verb with a real object. That is the difference between this and U menyá yest', where the thing is the subject and does not bend.
sentences.sound: DAY-tye pa-ZHA-loo-sta VO-doo. Both commas are pauses, and the middle word is where the politeness lives.

variations.changed: a masculine thing, so nothing bends — khleb stays as it is
a feminine thing, so M3's ending appears: knígu
a number in front, so the counting rule takes over: dva biléta

mistake.why: Dáyte takes an object, and a feminine -a noun bends as an object: vódu. It is M3's rule, in a shop.

sentences.usage: Ordering, asking, buying — the single most useful sentence frame in the course.
sentences.mnemonic: Dáyte takes an object, so the object bends. U menyá yest' takes a subject, so it does not.

words.note: One — and it is the only number besides dva that changes for gender: odín bilét, but odná kníga. After it the noun keeps its plain dictionary shape, which is what makes odín the easy end of the counting rule.

sentences.trap: Russian has no article, so odín is genuinely "one" and not "a". Putting it in front of every noun the way English puts "a" is the mistake — it counts, it does not introduce.
sentences.sound: a-DEEN bee-LYET pa-ZHA-loo-sta. The first o of odín is unstressed and flattens all the way to "a".

variations.changed: odín → odná for a feminine noun — the number agrees with what it counts
dva puts the noun into the 2–4 shape: biléta
the verb spelled out — and now bilét is an object, though a masculine one does not bend

mistake.why: kníga is feminine, so the number agrees with it: odná kníga.

sentences.usage: A ticket counter, a bakery, a market stall — the shortest complete purchase in the language.
sentences.mnemonic: odín is a count, not an article. Russian has no word for "a", and this is not it.

words.note: Two — the other number that changes for gender: dva biléta, but dve knígi. It puts the noun into the 2–4 shape, and tri and chetýre do exactly the same without changing themselves.

sentences.trap: Two endings are stacked here and only one of them is M3's. biléta is the 2–4 counting shape, not an object ending — the object ending would have been bilét, since masculine things do not bend as objects. The number wins.
sentences.sound: DAY-tye dva bee-LYE-ta pa-ZHA-loo-sta. The stress on biléta stays where it was in bilét.

variations.changed: dve for a feminine noun, and knígi for the 2–4 shape
odín, so the noun goes back to its plain shape

variations.cue: Two tickets cost a hundred roubles
variations.changed: the same number phrase as the subject — and stóyat, because there are two of them

mistake.why: dva puts the noun into the 2–4 shape: dva biléta. The counting rule overrides everything else in the sentence.

sentences.usage: Buying more than one of something — and the sentence where two rules meet and the number wins.
sentences.mnemonic: When a number and a verb both want the noun, the number gets it.

words.note: "More" or "another" when you are asking for a second helping, and "still" when something has not stopped. Written with yó, always, and the acute is part of that spelling rather than a choice: a Russian yó is the stressed vowel of its word by definition. The quiet line under it spells it ещё, with the two dots Russian print usually drops — which is one of the places the missing dots cost a beginner most, because the e-spelling hides both the sound and the stress.

sentences.trap: One small word covering "more", "another" and "still". Which one it means comes entirely from the situation, and asking which is which is the wrong question.
sentences.sound: ye-SHCHO chai pa-ZHA-loo-sta. The shch is a long soft "shch", and the yó is stressed, as every yó is.

variations.changed: a feminine noun after a verb that is understood, so M3's ending still appears: vódu
the verb spelled out, with yeshchyó between it and the thing
yeshchyó in front of a number — "one more", the commonest way it is used

mistake.why: ból'she is "more" in the sense of a larger quantity or a comparison. Asking for another helping is yeshchyó.

sentences.usage: A café, a table, a second helping — and the sentence that shows why the yó is worth writing out in full.
sentences.mnemonic: yeshchyó is the word for one more of what you already have.
